newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bertelsmann looks to youth for Internet century.
newsitem.headline: Bertelsmann looks to youth for Internet century.

text.p: Bertelsmann AG, Europe's biggest media conglomerate, said on Friday that the man who has driven the company's push into multimedia and Internet-related services would become the group's chairman next year.

The choice of Thomas Middelhoff, the 44-year-old board member in charge of corporate development and multimedia, to replace outgoing chairman Mark Woessner signals a generation change aimed at steering the group into the information age.

The company demonstratively pointed out in a statement that Middelhoff would maintain Bertelsmann's long tradition of a "balanced mix" of businesses ranging from book, newspaper and magazine publishing, to book clubs, television and new media.

But it was clear that Middelhoff's strengths in multimedia, particularly forming a European partnership with America Online, that secured his nomination to lead the group into the information industry that will dominate the next century.
"The American competition was already further advanced into cyberspace than Bertelsmann and other European rivals," the company said.
"This gap was closed through Middelhoff's initiative. Today Bertelsmann is present with substantial activities in the entire multimedia area," it added.
Middelhoff is an exhuberent, but methodical strategist.
Worried that Microsoft would roll over Europe with its planned Microsoft Network online service in 1995, Middelhoff formed a partnership with AOL, which now has some 600,000 subscribers in Europe.
Since then he has focused on adding key parts of the multimedia value chain from content production, network operation, intranet services to sales and distribution.
Woessner took the helm at Bertelsmann in 1983. Under company rules he must step down when he turns 60 on October 14, 1998.

Under his leadership Bertelsmann evolved from a sleepy European publishing and book club group with annual sales of around six billion marks ($3.4 billion) in the early 1980s into a global media player operating one of the world's biggest record companies and Europe's largest broadcasters by the end of 1996.
In the business year to June 30, 1996, sales totalled 21.5 billion marks and net income was 905 million marks.
The company last year completed the merger of its Ufa film and television group with Cie Luxembourgeoise de Telediffusion to form CLT/Ufa, Europe's biggest broadcaster.

Bertelsmann businesses include recording and entertaiment group BMG Entertainment, Buch AG book publishing and club division, Germany's biggest magazine publisher Gruner&Jahr, a huge printing division, and the New Media division which includes Bertelsmann AOL and Interactive Studios.

The main challengers facing Middelhoff for the top job at the world's third largest media group were Michael Dornemann, who heads the company's U.S.-based BMG Entertainment group, and finance chief Siegfried Luther.

But Luther is considered an old-school company executive and Dornemann is closely tied to New York, where BMG makes the largest contribution to Bertelsmann group sales. From his high-rise office on Times Square, Dornemann also oversees Bertelsmann's growing European television business.
"The centre of Dornemann's activities is in New York," a company official said. "Woessner would also have found it hard to replace him."
Middelhoff was also thought to be the preferred candidate of Reinhard Mohn, the grandfatherly figure who has gradually given up control of the company but still pulls strings.

Industry analysts said the choice for Middelhoff could signal a more risk-oriented shift in the company's strategy and probably a much stronger focus on Internet-related businesses that could involve stepped up investment.

"Investment has not been very large in this area. They have been growing these new businesses organically, but not really spending a lot of money," said Terry Povey, media analyst with HSBC James Capel.

One example of this is reports that Bertelsmann is adding cash to America Online Inc's offer to buy rival CompuServe Corp Inc. AOL's bid of about $1 billion in stock has so far been rejected by H&R Block Inc, which owns 80 percent of Compuserve.
"I think we will see more commitment from the company in the new media area," said Povey. ($ = 1.751 German Marks)
